memo:
Decision: all 125 affected people (70 in office and administrative support, 55 in business and financial operations) take the retrain-and-move-to-plant-role path at plant-role pay. No one takes the keep-current-pay path or severance.

Reasoning. The $11.4 million a year cost of the eliminated work is saved on every path, so the choice turns on what each path costs and what it fills. Moving at plant-role pay costs $60,600 per person once: $15,000 for retraining and $45,600 of pay and benefits during six months of training. Each mover fills a plant role the Company would otherwise fill by hiring from outside, at the same plant wage, so the ongoing plant payroll is unchanged. Retraining is paid back against outside hiring within two years, so over twenty years each move creates more value than elimination. Elimination costs only $8,902 in severance, but it leaves the plant vacancy to be filled by an outside hire at full hiring cost. The plants hire about 500 people a year, so 125 internal fills sit comfortably within that need.

Keeping current pay is dominated. It carries the same $60,600 one-time cost and adds a $16,560 average annual premium per person, about $2.1 million a year across 125 people. Over twenty years that premium outweighs any hiring saving, so this path destroys value.

Risks. Business and financial operations staff face a 39.8% pay cut at plant rates, which may prompt some to leave before they are productive. Office staff face a 1.5% cut, which is small. I will track attrition and training completion each quarter. If losses in business and financial operations run high, I will revisit severance for those who decline the move and report the result to the board.

I have decided that all 125 affected people (70 in office and administrative support, 55 in business and financial operations) will be retrained and moved into plant roles at plant-role pay.

The $11.4 million annual saving in work cost is achieved on every path, so the choice turns on the one-time and ongoing costs beyond that. Retraining costs $15,000 per person, plus about $45,600 per person in pay and benefits during six months of training. Against this, the plants would otherwise hire these roles from outside, and the retraining cost is recovered within two years compared with hiring from outside. Over a twenty-year horizon, that avoided hiring creates lasting value. Severance on elimination is cheaper upfront ($8,902 per person, about $1.1 million in total), but it produces no return and loses trained, experienced staff who could fill the 500 annual plant openings.

The keep-current-pay path adds $16,560 per person per year, about $2.1 million a year for all 125, for as long as they hold the plant role. Over twenty years that is more than $40 million undiscounted, and the pack identifies no offsetting retention or revenue benefit that would justify it. I have therefore allocated nothing to it.

The plant-pay path does reduce the pay of business and financial operations staff by about 40%, and this is a real retention risk. I will monitor acceptance and attrition closely, and the cash required (about $7.6 million for retraining and training pay) is covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. If a meaningful number of those staff decline, I will return to the board with a revised allocation, with severance as the fallback.

I have assigned all 125 affected people to the retrain-and-move path at plant pay, with none eliminated and none on keep-pay. The $11.4 million a year saving on the work is achieved on every path, so the choice turns on each person's one-off cost and on the outside hiring each move displaces.

Keep-pay is ruled out. It adds $16,560 a person a year, or about $2.1 million a year across 125 people. Over twenty years that is about $41 million undiscounted, or roughly $20 million in present value at 8%. Nothing in the pack offsets it.

Plant pay versus elimination. A move costs $15,000 of retraining plus about $45,600 of pay and benefits during six months of training, about $60,600 once per person. In return the Company does not have to hire that person from outside. The pack says the retraining cost is paid back against outside hiring in two years, which implies about $7,500 a year of avoided hiring cost. At 8% over twenty years, that stream is worth about $73,600 per person, so the move nets about $13,000 per person in present value. Elimination costs $8,902 in severance and gives no such return, so it is about $9,000 negative. The gap is roughly $22,000 per person, and it stays positive at a 10% discount rate.

The plants hire about 500 people a year, so 125 internal moves can be absorbed without idle capacity. Total one-off cost of about $7.6 million is covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. These are my estimates from the pack. The board should confirm the hiring-cost assumption, since the case rests on it.

The $11.4 million a year saved from removing this work applies on every path, so the choice turns on the people and the one-time and ongoing costs of each path. I have assigned all 125 to retraining and moving at plant-role pay.

Eliminate: $8,902 severance each, $1.1 million in total, and nothing further. It is the cheapest path today but creates no ongoing value, because the plants still need about 500 outside hires a year.

Plant pay: $60,600 per person once ($15,000 retraining plus $45,600 of pay during training), about $7.6 million in total. Each move fills a plant role the Company would otherwise hire for, so the retraining cost is recovered in two years. On the payback figure, the avoided hiring is worth about $7,500 a year, which continues over the twenty years. After the $8,902 of severance avoided, discounting at 10% leaves roughly $12,000 per person in favour of this path. That result depends on the benefit persisting, so it is sensitive to the assumption.

Keep current pay: $16,560 a person a year on average, $2.1 million a year at full take-up. That exceeds the roughly $7,500 annual benefit of retraining, so each such person costs shareholders money every year they hold the role. I assign none.

The cost is affordable: $7.6 million against $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level.

The main risk is to the people. Business and financial operations staff take a 39.8% pay cut on moving to plant pay, and office staff take 1.5%. That creates retention and fairness risk. If the board wishes to protect pay, it should fund that decision explicitly rather than through the keep-pay path, which is value-destroying on these figures.

Decision: all 125 affected people (70 office and administrative support, 55 business and financial operations) take the retrain-and-move path at plant-role pay.

Reasoning over the twenty-year horizon:

1. The $11.4 million annual saving from removing the work is the same on every path, so the choice turns on what each path costs beyond that saving.

2. Eliminating roles costs $8,902 per person once. It creates no ongoing cost, but it also fills no plant vacancy, so the Company must still hire 125 people from outside to meet its roughly 500 annual plant hires.

3. Retraining and moving at plant-role pay costs $15,000 per person for instruction plus $45,600 in pay and benefits during six months of training, about $60,600 once, or about $51,700 more than eliminating. In return, each person fills a role the Company would otherwise fill from outside. Retraining pays back in two years against hiring, implying roughly $7,500 a year of avoided hiring cost per person. Over twenty years that is about $150,000 undiscounted, or roughly $20,000 to $25,000 net of the extra one-time cost after discounting at 8% to 10%. The advantage is positive but modest, and it depends on the payback estimate holding.

4. Retraining and keeping current pay costs a further $16,560 a year per person, far more than the roughly $7,500 a year of avoided hiring cost. It destroys value over any reasonable horizon.

Plant-role pay is a large pay cut for business and financial staff (39.8%), which carries retention risk. The Company should monitor departures and offer support where needed, since lost retrained staff would erase the benefit.

Recommendation: move all 125 at plant-role pay.
